clusters.cluster: Symphony: the protocol, its evidence and its place

verdicts.quote_a: No server, database or daemon of the project's own: the forge is the lock, the CI is the scheduler, and the repository is the state.
verdicts.quote_b: Hosted pieces: nothing of ours runs. The webhook server is not deployed, and the Cloudflare sign-in service is approved but not built.
verdicts.explanation: The spec (2026-10-15) says Symphony's coordination has nothing to host. The handoff (2026-10-13) says the same thing, that nothing of the project's runs: the webhook server is not deployed and the sign-in service is not built. The two agree on what runs today. The handoff only adds two pieces that exist in code or in a plan.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the spec's 'nothing to host' for the coordination layer. Add the handoff's note that symphony-app's undeployed webhook stage (to be deleted) and the approved, unbuilt sign-in service for the control panel exist outside it.

verdicts.quote_a: Symphony makes a GitHub repository the coordinator of Claude Code agents, with no server of its own.
verdicts.quote_b: Coordination that runs in Actions with no server: unsorry and gh-aw do it too.
verdicts.explanation: The competitors note (2026-10-16) opens with this as a description, not as one of its three 'better by design' claims. The same note says 'Not unique alone: unsorry and gh-aw are serverless in Actions too' and puts 'Coordination in Actions with no server' under What not to claim, word for word as the spec (2026-10-15) does. The two documents agree.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry serverless coordination as shared with unsorry and gh-aw (spec section 8). Present only the combination of mechanisms as the claim.

verdicts.quote_a: Claude Pro's `setup-token` (a one-year OAuth credential, sanctioned for CI from the cheapest paid plan up)
verdicts.quote_b: Anthropic advises an API key for a secret shared across repositories and says plan limits "assume ordinary, individual usage"
verdicts.explanation: The ladder (2026-10-09) calls the setup-token 'sanctioned for CI'. The competitors note (2026-10-16) cites Anthropic's GitHub Actions and legal pages. Those pages document the token but advise an API key for a shared secret and leave open whether several workers on one plan count as ordinary use. The note also lists 'Anthropic approves agents on a subscription in CI' under what not to claim. The ladder's wording overstates what the later, sourced reading supports.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the competitors note's wording (also spec 9.5): Anthropic documents the token for claude-code-action, advises an API key for a shared secret, and question R6 is open. Drop 'sanctioned'.

verdicts.quote_a: Keep it one account. Rotating accounts or pooling several users' tokens to widen the window is the behaviour Anthropic's terms prohibit; if the workload needs more than one subscription's window, it is a workload for an API key.
verdicts.quote_b: The owner's own several Claude accounts may be coordinated from one orchestrator of the owner's, each worker on one account's token, knowing the terms question.
verdicts.explanation: The Slurm playbook (2026-10-03) calls rotating accounts to widen the usage window prohibited behaviour. The handoff (2026-10-13) designs a pool with one organization secret per account, SYMPHONY_CLAUDE_<NAME>, to spread runs over the owner's own accounts. It does this under an owner decision that names the terms question without settling it. The two pages disagree on whether this is allowed.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Record the pool as the owner's decision of 2026-10-13, taken knowing the terms question, not as compliant. Keep the playbook's statement as the opposing reading until Anthropic answers in writing (spec R6).

verdicts.quote_a: GITHUB\_TOKEN gets 1,000 requests an hour per repository and the library has no retry on 429 or secondary limits yet
verdicts.quote_b: GITHUB_TOKEN is limited to 1,000 API requests an hour per repository, 15,000 on Enterprise Cloud
verdicts.explanation: Both pages give 1,000 requests an hour per repository as the base limit. The handoff (2026-10-13) adds the Enterprise Cloud exception of 15,000. The spec (2026-10-15) states the general limit that applies to adopters on other plans. Read with their scopes, the two do not conflict.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry 1,000 an hour per repository, with the handoff's 15,000 on Enterprise Cloud. Note that the project's own organization is inferred to be on Enterprise Cloud.

verdicts.quote_a: **$17 a month** runs the whole machine: one Claude Pro seat, billed annually, beside a public repository on GitHub Free
verdicts.quote_b: sdlc-template is internal (Symphony constraint) and internal visibility belongs to organizations owned by an enterprise account, so the enterprise OpenGrid is an Enterprise Cloud account
verdicts.explanation: The ladder (2026-10-09) prices rungs for whoever adopts the template. It does not say which plan the project's own organization uses. The handoff (2026-10-13) infers the organization's own plan from internal visibility. The two pages answer different questions.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the ladder as adopter pricing. Carry the handoff's Enterprise Cloud reading, marked as inferred, as the project's own plan.

verdicts.quote_a: the board's cron fallback cut from hourly to six-hourly, saving a private repository about 630 billed minutes a month
verdicts.quote_b: sdlc-template-test board.yml (cron '17 * * * *') 16 scheduled runs from 2026-10-09T09:11Z to 2026-10-13T00:42Z (~87 slots)
verdicts.explanation: The ladder (2026-10-09) prices the hourly fallback at about 750 minutes a month and the six-hourly one at about 120. That arithmetic assumes every cron slot runs. The handoff (2026-10-13) measured an hourly board cron that ran 16 of about 87 slots and a ten-minute sweep that ran 8 of about 300. It concludes that schedules 'ran hours late and dropped most slots'. The 630-minute saving therefore rests on a firing rate the measurement contradicts.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the handoff's measured run counts. Give the ladder's minute figures only as upper bounds that assume every slot fires; a month of billed minutes for the board workflow would settle the real cost.

verdicts.quote_a: A fix that reads GitHub's own record of the push is written but not merged (finding F8)
verdicts.quote_b: The fix merged on main on 2026-10-15 reads GitHub's record of the push; one gap remains, a claim's first push, and the fix is unreleased.
verdicts.explanation: The manual of 2026-10-15 and the spec's risk 13 say the F8 fix is written but not merged. The competitors note of 2026-10-16 reads symphony-protocol main at b4c3c1a. It says #35 merged on 2026-10-15, is unreleased, and leaves one gap. The later reading revises the earlier status.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the competitors note: the F8 fix (#35) is merged on main as of 2026-10-15 and unreleased, a claim's first push is still open, and 0.4.1 and every copy still read the committer date.

verdicts.quote_a: against an oracle written from the spec's text: 16.7 million states at depth 8 and 18.8 million with two issues at depth 7
verdicts.quote_b: This is bounded checking of small worlds, not a proof.
verdicts.explanation: The competitors note's 'exhaustively' means every interleaving up to a stated depth. The note gives those depths (8 on one issue, 7 on two) and a depth-5 search in the required check. The brief (2026-10-14) describes the same method as bounded checking of small worlds. Neither page claims a proof, so the two agree once the bound is read.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry 'exhaustive within a depth bound, not a proof': depth 5 in the required check, and depth 8 on one issue and 7 on two in the deep searches (spec, manual).

verdicts.quote_a: the prototype found twelve defects, F1 to F12
verdicts.quote_b: found 19 defects: six are fixed in release 0.4.1, eleven more on main ahead of the next release, one (F16) was settled by changing the spec, and one (F8, idleness read from the committer date) waits on the owner
verdicts.explanation: The handoff's count (2026-10-13) covers the prototype's findings F1 to F12. By 2026-10-15 the spec counts 19 defects from building the harness and reviewing its fixes, broken down by status. The brief of 2026-10-14 already names F13 to F17. The later count supersedes the earlier one.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry 19 defects from the spec (2026-10-15), with its breakdown. Update the F8 status from the competitors note (fix merged on main on 2026-10-15).

verdicts.quote_a: found 19 defects: six are fixed in release 0.4.1, eleven on main but not yet released, one was settled in the spec, and one (F8) is open
verdicts.quote_b: 0.4.1 of 2026-10-13 is the last release, and twelve fixes made since are on main and unreleased (a thirteenth finding, F16, was settled in the spec), so an adopter waits for 0.5.0
verdicts.explanation: The manual (2026-10-15) counts 6 in 0.4.1, 11 on main, F16 in the spec and F8 open. The competitors note (2026-10-16) counts twelve on main. That is the eleven plus F8, whose fix #35 it says merged on 2026-10-15. The totals agree at 19, and the later note moves F8 onto main.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the competitors note: twelve fixes on main and unreleased, F16 settled in the spec, and 0.4.1 the last release, as of 2026-10-16.

verdicts.quote_a: 59 deliberately broken copies of the rules (mutants) are each caught
verdicts.quote_b: 93 mutants, copies of the library each broken on purpose, were each caught, 109 on main after #35
verdicts.explanation: The brief counts 59 mutants at symphony-protocol b5f098d (2026-10-14). The spec (2026-10-15) says 93, and the competitors note (2026-10-16) says 93, then 109 on main after #35. The count grows with later commits. The pages do not say whether 93 includes the deep lane's mutants.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry 109 on main after #35 (competitors note, 2026-10-16), with 59 at b5f098d and 93 in the spec as earlier counts. validation/mutants.py at a named commit would fix the scope.

verdicts.quote_a: two workers on one issue to depth 5 (about 29,500 states), three workers to depth 4, and every fault kind from a due claim. None found a violation
verdicts.quote_b: Its fast lane, a search to depth 5, is part of the required check; the deep searches run weekly or by hand, not as required checks
verdicts.explanation: The brief describes the fast lane run in the required check. The spec's 16.7 and 18.8 million states come from the deep searches in the run of record of 2026-10-14. The spec (5.3) and the manual both name the two lanes separately. These are two searches, not a revised figure for one.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry both, each named by lane: depth 5 (about 29,500 states) in the required check, and depth 8 (16.7 million) and depth 7 with two issues (18.8 million) in the deep searches.

verdicts.quote_a: On symphony-protocol's main today (b5f098d, after F15 and F16 merged this evening), 12 hold, 2 hold only if commit dates are honest, 1 is known broken, 1 is partly checked and 1 is not checked.
verdicts.quote_b: on 2026-10-15 the local push guard was found to judge a lease (a forced push that fails if the branch has moved since) by its own directory rather than the clone a git -C push names (risk 12)
verdicts.explanation: The brief's tally holds for b5f098d (2026-10-14). By 2026-10-16 the competitors note reads main at b4c3c1a. On main, #35 has replaced the commit-date clock that the two conditional guarantees (G2, G3) rested on. A push-guard defect found on 2026-10-15 also bears on G11a, which the brief lists as holding. No later page recounts the seventeen guarantees.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the brief's tally only as of b5f098d. A recount of validation/GUARANTEES.md at b4c3c1a or later would give the current figures.

verdicts.quote_a: 42 pairs give 80 percent power only for differences of about 26 to 30 points
verdicts.quote_b: At 50 pairs it can detect a gap of about 25 points
verdicts.explanation: The handoff (2026-10-13) sizes the run on the pairs it knew would grade, 'every pre-registered flash pair that grades (42 known, up to 50)'. The brief (2026-10-14) quotes the pre-registered 50. The two power figures are for different denominators and are consistent with each other. Neither page revises the other.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the 50 pre-registered pairs (brief) and the handoff's finding that 42 of them grade in the cloud session, each with its own detectable gap.

verdicts.quote_a: 50 pairs from 20 tasks, five arms (sdlc, solo, coop, coop-git, team)
verdicts.quote_b: The coordbench full run you chose on 2026-10-15 (35 new pairs under five arms, plus the runs to redo)
verdicts.explanation: The brief (2026-10-14) gives the pre-registered plan of 50 pairs. The spec records a later choice of the owner's, made on 2026-10-15: 35 new pairs under five arms plus the runs to redo, judged against a roughly 15-point noise floor. Neither page gives the total number of pairs for the chosen run.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the spec's description of the chosen run (2026-10-15). coordbench's PLAN.md or run record would give the total pair count.

verdicts.quote_a: The one real pair on record is a smoke run of the coop arm, which did not pass and says nothing about Symphony
verdicts.quote_b: has run 8 pairs: Symphony's arm passed 6 of 8 like every two-agent arm, one agent 5 of 8, and no difference is significant
verdicts.explanation: The brief reads coordbench at 5e4860e (2026-10-14), when one smoke pair was on record. By 2026-10-15 the spec reports an 8-pair step. On 2026-10-16 the competitors note adds that 11 of that step's 40 runs were spoiled, so its figures are not reportable.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry: a pilot and an 8-pair step have run, and the step's figures are not reportable after the harness audit (competitors note, 2026-10-16). Quote no pass counts.

verdicts.quote_a: Symphony's arm passed 6 of 8 like every two-agent arm, one agent 5 of 8, and no difference is significant (every exact McNemar p is 1.000
verdicts.quote_b: its harness audit found 11 of that step's 40 runs spoiled (a full disk, a pair spawned twice), so its figures are not reportable
verdicts.explanation: The spec (2026-10-15) reports the 8-pair step's pass counts and McNemar p values. The competitors note (2026-10-16) reports the later harness audit: 11 of the step's 40 runs were spoiled, and its figures are not reportable until the reruns and the full run complete.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the competitors note: the 8-pair step's figures are not reportable. Leave the 6 of 8 and 5 of 8 counts out, as the grant hold also requires.

verdicts.quote_a: Giving each pair a git server moved success by only 1 to 3 points (Verified, the February 2026 post in the cooperbench/website repository).
verdicts.quote_b: messages only 26%, solo 48%, a shared git remote 56%, a team with a lead and a shared task list 62%
verdicts.explanation: The spec gives two figures for adding git to message-only pairs: 1 to 3 points in the February 2026 post, and 26% to 56% in the later ablation (50 pairs, one seed, one model). The handoff labels the second gap 'coop 26 against coop-git 56'. The spec sets both in one bullet without reconciling them, and the brief carries only the ablation. They give conflicting sizes for the same manipulation.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry both, each with its sample: the post's 1 to 3 points, and the ablation's 30 points as weak evidence (n = 50, one seed). The two setups as the post and the ablation describe them would show whether they test the same thing.

verdicts.quote_a: Plain `sbatch` templates through the existing adapter (recommended for phase 2: no new dependency, works on CentOS 7) or Metaflow with `metaflow-slurm`
verdicts.quote_b: **Chosen, not built.** Metaflow is the chosen engine, but metaflow-slurm drives sbatch over SSH with a key file
verdicts.explanation: The roadmap (2026-10-03) recommends plain sbatch for phase 2, with Metaflow as an option. The manual and spec (2026-10-15) say Metaflow is chosen but not built. They add that metaflow-slurm drives sbatch over SSH with a key file, against Beethoven's credential rule, unless a planned plain sbatch adapter replaces it.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the spec and manual (2026-10-15): Metaflow chosen, not built, with the metaflow-slurm credential caveat and the planned plain sbatch adapter.

verdicts.quote_a: The module numbers follow the project topic's own mapping and have not been checked against the REFORMS paper (Kapoor et al., 2024); confirming them is a phase 3 task.
verdicts.quote_b: The goal text's mapping comes from "02-Autonomous AI HPC Architecture" in the Beethoven-notebook folder.
verdicts.explanation: The roadmap's statement is about the module numbers in its own table of controls, which come from the project's mapping. The checklist (same day) takes its own item list from the REFORMS paper and confirms the module names on the REFORMS site. It also says the goal text's mapping comes from the project's own document. The two cover different lists and do not conflict.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the checklist's 32 items as taken from the paper. Mark the roadmap's control-to-module numbering as unchecked until its phase 3 check.

verdicts.quote_a: On Windows, `python3 --version` must print a version in Git Bash, or the plugin's push guard silently does nothing.
verdicts.quote_b: the push guard now refuses a push when it cannot run (the Windows Store's python3 stub made it pass every push)
verdicts.explanation: Both pages are dated 2026-10-13. The onboarding describes a guard that passes silently when Python cannot run. The handoff records symphony-marketplace#10 (plugin 0.1.7), merged that night, under which the guard refuses the push instead. The handoff also says spine-program's sessions get 0.1.7 at the plugin's next update.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the handoff: since plugin 0.1.7 the guard fails closed when Python cannot run. The onboarding's line holds only for an older plugin that has not updated.

verdicts.quote_a: spine-program, the repository the packet builds on, adopted Symphony's protocol alone on 2026-10-12, according to the template's checkpoints
verdicts.quote_b: spine-program adopted the protocol only, on 2026-10-12 at 01:09Z (fd49afa).
verdicts.explanation: The handoff gives both '2026-10-11 (pull request #1)' and '2026-10-12 at 01:09Z (fd49afa)', so it carries the spec's date itself. 01:09 UTC on 2026-10-12 is the evening of 2026-10-11 in the owner's local time. The two dates most likely name one adoption reckoned in two time zones.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry 2026-10-12 at 01:09 UTC (commit fd49afa, pull request #1), and note that it is the evening of 2026-10-11 locally.

verdicts.quote_a: 4 of 4 copies on 0.4.1, plugin 0.1.10
verdicts.quote_b: Its `tools/VENDORED` says `sdlc-protocol 0.2.0 f530a66`, not 0.3.x as the brief has it; `vendoring.py verify` passes on 15 files.
verdicts.explanation: The handoff's '4 of 4' counts the four consumers on the sync's list: symphony-template, symphony-marketplace, symphony-app and coordbench ('The four consumers ... The sync of 0.4.1 into every copy'). spine-program is an adopted repository with no protocol.yml, outside that list. Read by scope, both statements hold.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry 'the four consumers on 0.4.1, plugin 0.1.10' and, separately, spine-program frozen at 0.2.0 with no protocol.yml (handoff, 2026-10-13).

verdicts.quote_a: Benchmark Symphony's claim protocol with coordbench's existing sdlc arm, run in coordbench's own GitHub Actions on GitHub-hosted runners
verdicts.quote_b: A benchmark that runs other projects' tasks, and a paid App whose runtime rides each customer's free minutes, need a reading (Open, question R5).
verdicts.explanation: The handoff (2026-10-13) recommends the benchmark on GitHub-hosted runners without discussing GitHub's Actions terms. The spec (2026-10-15) quotes the terms' limit on hosted runners to the repository's own software project and makes this case an open question. A recommendation and an open question do not settle whether the design is permitted.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the design together with open question R5. GitHub's written answer, or a lawyer's reading, on coordbench running other projects' tasks would settle it.

verdicts.quote_a: the ladder below was verified against GitHub's and Anthropic's own pages on Oct 9, 2026.
verdicts.quote_b: Plan prices: the only ones in the docs come from the plan changes of April 14, 2020: Pro $4 a month, Team $4 per user a month. Whether those are still current is not confirmed.
verdicts.explanation: The ladder (2026-10-09) presents its rungs, GitHub Pro at $4 among them, as verified against GitHub's pages. The handoff's free-or-paid table (2026-10-13) found the $4 prices only in docs from April 2020 and could not confirm them, since github.com/pricing could not be read. The two disagree on whether the price is verified.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry $4 for Pro and $4 a user for Team as GitHub's docs price of 2020, not confirmed current (handoff). A read of GitHub's pricing page with its date would verify it.

verdicts.quote_a: None of these gates exists yet: both repositories today are the Remote Control launcher (hpcworker framework 11, extension 12.0.0)
verdicts.quote_b: - **Beethoven (23.x).** It has one `worker_name` and one `project_url`.
verdicts.explanation: The checklist dates extension 12.0.0 to 2026-10-03. The note of 2026-10-21 puts Beethoven at 23.x. On 2026-10-15 the spec still had 20.0.0 as pre-release. The version moved over time.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry Beethoven 23.x as of 2026-10-21 (several grid workers note), with 12.0.0 as the 2026-10-03 state.

verdicts.quote_a: hpcworker framework 11, extension 12.0.0
verdicts.quote_b: the grid answers with framework 22.
verdicts.explanation: The checklist (2026-10-03) has hpcworker at framework 11. The grid review read framework 22 from the grid at 12:03 UTC on 2026-10-21, and the several-workers note of the same day speaks of framework 22-23.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry framework 22, read 2026-10-21 (grid review), with 11 as the 2026-10-03 state.

verdicts.quote_a: tagged `v2.0.0` at its merge commit (53d5ae5) on 2026-10-07. A session may not create tags.
verdicts.quote_b: main is at 5.0.0, but only v1.0.0 to v3.0.0 are tagged.
verdicts.explanation: On 2026-10-07 the latest tag was v2.0.0. The handoff of 2026-10-13 finds main at 5.0.0 with tags only up to v3.0.0, and beethoven-agents pinned to v3.0.0, and it asks the owner to tag v4.0.0 and v5.0.0. The spec of 2026-10-15 says the same.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry: main at 5.0.0, last tag v3.0.0, v4.0.0 and v5.0.0 tags waiting on the owner (handoff 2026-10-13, spec 2026-10-15).

verdicts.quote_a: Triggers: GitHub pull request events on this repo, an API trigger, and an hourly schedule.
verdicts.quote_b: (about 120 minutes a month, cut from about 750 when it was hourly)
verdicts.explanation: The plan of 2026-10-08 runs a coordinator routine hourly. By 2026-10-09 the board is a workflow whose cron fallback was cut from hourly to six-hourly (sdlc-template#7). The brief and the spec later say every six hours.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry a six-hourly fallback for the board's run (ladder 2026-10-09, brief, spec), with events as the main trigger.

verdicts.quote_a: a task is claimed by pushing a branch named after its Linear issue (`claude/LIN-123`).
verdicts.quote_b: chose GitHub Issues and asked for the repository side first, as a GitHub template repository built from the bottom up with no export or import in its first layer
verdicts.explanation: The plan of 2026-10-08 makes Linear the queue, with claude/LIN-123 branches. The build plan records that on 2026-10-09 the owner chose GitHub Issues and left Linear for later. Every later page uses issues and claude/N.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry GitHub Issues as the queue and claude/N as the claim branch, from the owner's choice of 2026-10-09. Linear is history.

verdicts.quote_a: GPT-5 315 against 183 of 652 (48.3% against 28.1%), Claude Sonnet 4.5 307 against 168 (47.1% against 25.8%).
verdicts.quote_b: one GPT-5 agent passed 315 of 652 feature pairs where two agents passed 183
verdicts.explanation: Both pages carry the same CooperBench count, and the manual cites the spec's 7.1 for it. The spec read the count from the paper's PDF in the authors' repository. These are one sourced claim repeated, not two confirmations.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the counts once, from the spec (Verified, paper PDF), quoting counts rather than percentages.

verdicts.quote_a: messages only 26%, solo 48%, a shared git remote 56%, a team with a lead and a shared task list 62%
verdicts.quote_b: In CooperBench's later ablation (50 pairs, one seed, one model) messaging alone reached 26%, one agent 48%, a shared git remote 56%, and a lead with a shared task list and scratchpad 62%
verdicts.explanation: Both pages give the same four figures from CooperBench's ablation. The brief takes them through coordbench's research.md, and the spec from the CooperBench repository at 63b9d44. They are one claim carried twice, and both call it weak evidence (n = 50, one seed).
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the figures once, from the spec (CooperBench at 63b9d44), with its caveat of 50 pairs, one seed and one model.

verdicts.quote_a: The workflow token's 1,000 requests an hour per repository, the 100-run concurrency queue and 20 concurrent jobs on GitHub Free probably bind before minutes do, and the library has no retry on 429 yet
verdicts.quote_b: Probably GitHub's API limits, though nobody has measured it: 1,000 requests an hour on GITHUB\_TOKEN, 100 queued runs, 20 concurrent jobs on Free, and no retry on 429 in the library yet
verdicts.explanation: The two pages carry the same list of limits and the same guess. Both point back to the spec's 9.3, risk 5 and question R3. It is one unmeasured inference repeated.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry it once as the spec's inference, unmeasured until question R3's measurement pass.

verdicts.quote_a: 2,000 included minutes a month on Free, 3,000 on Pro and Team, 50,000 on Enterprise Cloud, then $0.006 a minute on Linux (since 2026-01-01)
verdicts.quote_b: private repositories get 2,000, 3,000 or 50,000 included minutes a month, then $0.006 a minute on Linux since 2026-01-01
verdicts.explanation: The manual's deep-research prompt restates the spec's runner, concurrency and minutes figures, which the spec read from github/docs at 12691d2 on 2026-10-15. It is the same set of figures, not a second check.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the figures once, from spec 9.2 to 9.4 (github/docs at 12691d2, 2026-10-15).

verdicts.quote_a: On a private repository on Team it is 15,000 minutes over the quota, about $90 a month, before the board's own runs
verdicts.quote_b: in the spec's illustration, ten one-hour Claude runs a day come to about $90 a month on Team (spec 9.4)
verdicts.explanation: The manual attributes the $90 to the spec's illustration. The spec grades it Inferred, with the workload assumed. It is one illustration repeated, and the manual drops the grade.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the $90 once, as the spec's illustration graded Inferred, with its assumed workload stated.

verdicts.quote_a: Deleted two hours after the claim by a reaper every 15 minutes; the work is not kept
verdicts.quote_b: its reaper workflow for the sweep every 15 minutes, and tools/gate\_b/config.py (TTL\_SECONDS = 7200) for the two-hour TTL, re-read 2026-10-15.
verdicts.explanation: The spec and the competitors note carry the same unsorry figures, a two-hour TTL and a 15-minute reaper. Both also give gh-aw's 68 broken TLA+ configurations. Both rest on the 2026-10-15 reads (verify/01 and verify/03, unsorry at 029d328b), which the note cites. They are one sourced claim, not two confirmations.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the figures once, citing unsorry at 029d328b and gh-aw at dc91dbed as read on 2026-10-15.

verdicts.explanation: Both pages are dated 2026-09-18 and describe the same held-out real-film test with the same sentence: three misses in 243, two of them the sacrum. Naming Vertebrae Without CT says the detector finds 97.6%, while Vertebral Levels Without CT says 99.2%. Three of 243 is 98.8%, which matches neither.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry 'three misses in 243 (two the sacrum)' and no percentage until the detector's evaluation file is read.

verdicts.quote_a: the miss rate is 2.42% at confidence 0.25, 0.10 and 0.05 alike
verdicts.quote_b: it misses only 2.2% of vertebrae — but 17.9% come out duplicated
verdicts.explanation: Naming's 2.42% agrees with Vertebral Levels' own threshold table (2.4% at each threshold). Vertebral Levels' 2.2% with 17.9% duplication sits in a paragraph about the detector on 25 held-out radiographs used for sweep chains, and the page does not say it is the same set. Naming reports duplication differently, as 3.03% within frames and 21.8% across frames.
verdicts.resolution_hint: The detector evaluation record for each set (the 243-vertebra test and the 25-film sweep set) would settle which miss rate goes with which; carry 2.4% for the threshold test meanwhile.

verdicts.quote_a: Lumbar real films, n=24 78.7% alone 93.6% swept
verdicts.quote_b: 78.7% without the sweep · n=25 films
verdicts.explanation: Naming Vertebrae Without CT's chart and Vertebral Levels Without CT's own chart both give the lumbar real-film row as n=24 at 78.7% alone and 93.6% swept. Vertebral Levels' headline tile gives the same 78.7% at n=25 films. One page holds two n's for one row.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry n=24 (both charts) provisionally; the evaluation record behind the row would settle it.

verdicts.quote_a: Trained on the 4,526 images that carry a sacrum box, single class, split by patient: precision 98.2%, recall 96.9%
verdicts.quote_b: 5,110 images carry a sacrum box and zero carry an S1 box

The page does not reconcile the two: 4,526 may be the training side of a patient split of 5,110, or a different snapshot.

verdicts.quote_a: 56 VerSeFusion (50 with an L6, 6 with a T13)
verdicts.quote_b: VerSe scans with L6: 85 scans (Liebl 2021) against 47 cases (Sekuboyina 2021) and 87 read series. No file has counted from the masks.

verdicts.quote_a: CTSpinoPelvic1K L6: 18 by release label, 16 by the readers' own count, 29 persons in the registry.

The Reality Check itself lists CTSpinoPelvic1K as holding 18 L6. So 34 is not an L6 count and does not contradict a. The State of the Literature's own disagreement (18, 16 or 29) is real but internal to it.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry 18 by release label, 16 by the readers and 29 in the registry as an open disagreement (State of the Literature), and do not cite 34 as an L6 count.

verdicts.quote_a: 802 records, one per patient; 422 supine, 377 prone

verdicts.quote_a: called L5 in 41 of 68

verdicts.quote_a: It moves with computing budget — 100% at 200 restarts, 99.3% at 50 — which is the signature of a convergence rate
verdicts.quote_b: the 'registration-based tools report near-perfect accuracy' summary (Otake 99.99%, Lo 100%/99.3%, Vaishnav 100%) were both voted down
verdicts.explanation: Vertebral Levels Without CT (2026-09-18) presents LevelCheck's 99.998% and its 100% / 99.3% as registration convergence rates checked against their sources. The feasibility study (2026-09-15; its caveats are rendered one character per line) says that same near-perfect summary was voted down. It keeps only labels within the correct level on all 398 radiographs after 21 exclusions, and a 42.2% helpfulness whose region parts sum to 157, not 168. The pages agree that none of these is naming accuracy but disagree on whether the registration figures survived verification.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the feasibility study's verified LevelCheck facts (labels in the correct level on 398 radiographs after 21 exclusions; helpful in 42.2% as a three-surgeon mean), and keep 99.998%, 100% and 99.3% out unless re-verified.

verdicts.quote_a: the comparator 97.6 % cannot be exceeded at any reachable n
verdicts.quote_b: LevelCheck H2, superiority over 97.6 % | as H1 | 0 below 152 persons at any accuracy | 708 at a true 99 %; never at 98 %
verdicts.explanation: Both pages are dated 2026-10-08 and both make the claim, but the State of the Literature gives its basis in the power table: zero power below 152 persons, 708 needed at a true 99%, never reached at 98%. Research Directions repeats 152 and 708. The calculation is on the page, and both name the same paper-2 comparator against registration-assisted surgeons.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the claim with the State of the Literature's H2 power row as its basis, and the comparator as Manbachi 2018's 97.6% assisted reading of 62 hard films (Research Directions).

verdicts.quote_b: Rule counting decoder on CT truth | 6 of 6 L6 found; 2 of 3 sacralisations over-counted | measured, CT only
verdicts.explanation: Research Directions (2026-10-08) still lists 'CT-7, the anchor-ordinal design' with arms 1 and 2 as a matched pair to run, so the spec's arms remain unrun as the spec says. It reads the 0.990 as a within-patient number, which agrees with the spec's 'each patient's own size divided out'. The 6 of 6 L6 belongs to a rule counting decoder on CT truth, a different mechanism. The spec's state still holds, so it is not stale.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the 0.990 as a within-patient, case-median-normalised separability (Research Directions) and the anchor-ordinal arms as unrun.

results.label: verify:2:The case for the OR study: propo

clusters.cluster: The case for the OR study: proposal, seed grant and IRB protocols

verdicts.quote_a: A detector trained on renders of DeepFluoro's own CTs finds the sacrum on 90–97% of the real frames, six specimens held out in turn.
verdicts.quote_b: A detector trained only on calibrated renders of DeepFluoro's own CTs finds the sacrum on about 96–98% of real frames (leave-one-specimen-out).
verdicts.explanation: The September 2026 proposal tables 90-97% for the population-matched detector (six specimens, three seeds) and says every synthetic number is from the leave-one-specimen-out runs of 21 September 2026. The October 2026 grant describes the same experiment and gives about 96-98%, with no new run named. The OR readiness ledger of 22 September gives 88.5-91.3% as the clean render-only figure for specimen 18-1109, which sits with the lower range, not the grant's.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry 90-97% from Counting Levels Under Fluoroscopy, the figure tied to the dated runs and a named report tool. Use 96-98% only if a run record for it turns up.

verdicts.quote_a: nine calibrated device terms add 4.3 points, held out by specimen
verdicts.quote_b: nine device terms fitted on 255 real frames including all 104 of 18-1109
verdicts.explanation: The grant's 4.3 points is the gain in variance explained, measured with held-out folds. The ledger's own device-card section (22 September 2026) says the nine terms are fitted leave-one-group-out and reproduce the shipped calibration folds, and the proposal's figure uses terms fitted with that specimen left out. The 255-frame fit that the ledger flags is a different thing: the calibration behind one render-only detector's training renders (anchor_none_v2_17-1882), listed as that detector's exposure to the test specimen. The two statements are about different fits.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Keep the grant's held-out 4.3-point variance gain. Report the ledger's init-exposure flag separately, as a caveat on detectors trained from the anchor_none_v2 renders, not on the calibration figure.

verdicts.quote_a: read correctly, physics alone explains 86% of a real frame rather than 80%, and the calibrated renderer about 90% of a held-out one.
verdicts.quote_b: our renderer explains 80.9% of a real frame's variance
verdicts.explanation: The September 2026 proposal first gives 81% for physics alone, then corrects it: the stored DeepFluoro frames were log-compressed display images, and read correctly physics explains 86% and the calibrated renderer about 90% of a held-out frame. The October 2026 grant, and the retrospective protocol after it, still give 80.9% and say nothing of the correction. So the later documents carry the figure the earlier one withdrew.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the corrected reading from Counting Levels Under Fluoroscopy (86% physics alone, about 90% calibrated on held-out frames). Mark the grant's and protocol's 80.9% as the figure from before the correction.

verdicts.quote_a: nine calibrated device terms add +4
verdicts.quote_b: | Siemens Cios Fusion (DeepFluoro) | | 366 | | 0.899 → 0.905 (+1.3) |
verdicts.explanation: The proposal's +4 sits on an 81% physics baseline. The ledger's Cios Fusion card (22 September 2026) gives held-out R² from 0.899 physics to 0.905 fitted, labelled +1.3, which is a different baseline. The card's 0.006 rise does not even match its own +1.3 label, so the column may be in other units. The texts do not show that the two figures measure the same quantity.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Settle it with the device-fit output for the Cios Fusion card, which defines the R² space and the +1.3 column, compared with the variance measure behind the 81%/+4 (and the grant's 80.9%/+4.3).

verdicts.quote_a: renders of living whole-body CTs (baseline; two renderings of the protocol) | | 64% / 77%
verdicts.quote_b: The manuscript's 76.9% belongs to the anchor_none_r2 generation; the v2 generation every real fine-tune started from pools to 64.0%.
verdicts.explanation: The proposal calls 64% and 77% two renderings of the protocol. The ledger (22 September 2026) assigns 76.9% and 64.0% to two detector generations, r2 and v2, and the grant says 64-77% depending on round. A new generation may come with new renders, so 'renderings' and 'generations' could name the same change. Neither page says whether the renders, the detector or both changed between the two.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Settle it with the training records of anchor_none_r2 and anchor_none_v2, showing whether they differ in renders, in the detector, or in both. Until then, carry both values with the ledger's generation labels.

verdicts.quote_a: the Fourier low-band swap added about ten points, the high-pass refiner and the full refiner about eight
verdicts.quote_b: Learned refiners and Fourier low-band swaps are being measured as arms; results are pending.
verdicts.explanation: The September 2026 proposal reports the refiner and low-band-swap arms as measured on six folds with three seeds each (74% and 72% against the 64%/77% baseline) and says each gain is smaller than the 26-point seed spread. The October 2026 grant says the same arms are still being measured, with results pending. The later document calls pending a result the earlier one already reports.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the measured results from Counting Levels Under Fluoroscopy, with its caveat that every gain is inside the seed spread. Drop the grant's 'results are pending'.

verdicts.quote_a: A RealDRR-style refiner trained on the real pairs, a high-pass-only version of it, and a training-free low-band swap
verdicts.quote_b: Render-to-fluoro translation (SDXL, CUT, CycleGAN, ADDA) | no gain in any arm | refuted
verdicts.explanation: The 8 October 2026 note marks as refuted a named set of image-translation methods: SDXL, CUT, CycleGAN and ADDA restyling. The proposal's arms are other methods: a RealDRR-style refiner, its high-pass version and a Fourier low-band swap. The proposal itself also says no gain exceeds the 26-point seed spread, so single-run differences do not exist. The two pages are about different arms and do not conflict.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry both, each with its own scope: the translation methods named in Research Directions gave no gain, and the refiner and low-band arms in Counting Levels gave gains of 8-10 points that sit inside seed noise.

verdicts.quote_a: Exactness is regional: 99.7% lumbar and 95.5% thoracic from the sacrum; 83.8% cervical in the one arm that reaches that far.
verdicts.quote_b: 99.33/97.41/83.84% lumbar/thoracic/cervical on the 522
verdicts.explanation: The proposal's 99.7% and 95.5% round the grant's 801-spine figures (99.73% and 95.45%). Its cervical figure is labelled as coming from 'the one arm that reaches that far', which is the grant's 522-spine arm at 83.84%. The values agree. The proposal simply leaves out that arm's 97.41% thoracic figure.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the grant's per-arm figures: 99.73/95.45% (lumbar/thoracic) on 801 spines and 99.33/97.41/83.84% on 522, each named with its arm.

verdicts.quote_a: 81% of events are a count that went wrong under fluoroscopy
verdicts.quote_b: with image misinterpretation named in 18.8%
verdicts.explanation: The grant gives the registry's cause as 'intraoperative disorientation' in 81.3%. The proposal and the visual abstract read that as a fluoroscopic count gone wrong. The 15 September 2026 protocol draft says image misinterpretation was named in 18.8%, and the two shares sum to about 100%, which suggests separate categories. Whether a miscount under fluoroscopy belongs to 'disorientation' or to 'image misinterpretation' depends on the registry paper's definitions, which no page quotes.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Settle it with the cause categories and definitions in the 2026 registry paper of 34,544 operations (Bone Joint J 2026). Until then, carry '81.3% intraoperative disorientation' in the grant's own words.

verdicts.quote_a: in 0.42% of thoracic cases, and every event was at L4–5 or L5–S1
verdicts.quote_b: thoracic 0.42%, 1 in 240
verdicts.explanation: The 15 September 2026 protocol draft gives a thoracic rate of 0.42% in the same sentence where it says every event was at L4-5 or L5-S1, which cannot both hold. The visual abstract and the grant both give thoracic 0.42% (1 in 240), and the grant adds lumbar 0.13% and cervical 0.05%. The draft's claim that every event was lumbosacral contradicts the regional rates.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the regional rates from the grant and the visual abstract. Drop 'every event was at L4-5 or L5-S1' unless the registry paper supports it for some subset.

verdicts.quote_a: Wrong-level spine surgery occurred in 0.12% of 34,544 consecutive cases in a recent single-system series
verdicts.quote_b: In a registry of 34,544 degenerative spine operations at 27 hospitals (2012–2022) the incidence was 0.12% (95% CI 0.09–0.16)
verdicts.explanation: Both give the same 0.12% of 34,544 operations. The draft calls the source a single-system series; the grant, and the later protocol, call it a registry at 27 hospitals over 2012-2022. One health system can run 27 hospitals, so the descriptions may not conflict, and neither page says how the hospitals are organised.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Settle it with the methods section of the 2026 registry paper. Carry the grant's fuller description (27 hospitals, 2012-2022, 95% CI 0.09-0.16).

verdicts.quote_a: 15% of surgeons have prepared the wrong level and caught it before incision, and nearly one in five has been sued for it
verdicts.quote_b: Almost 50% of 569 AANS/CNS Spine Section respondents had done one and nearly 20% had been sued for it
verdicts.explanation: The retrospective protocol shows that the 15% who prepared the wrong level and caught it comes from the 2008 survey of 415 surgeons. The 'nearly one in five sued' matches the grant's 2013 survey, in which nearly 20% of 569 respondents had been sued: a share of surgeons, not of events. The abstract cites both surveys, and its cost model correctly applies the per-event 17% litigated to events. The figures agree once read with their sources.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the three figures with their own surveys: 15% caught before incision (2008 survey), 17% of 418 events litigated (2008 survey, per event), nearly 20% of 569 respondents sued (2013 survey, per surgeon).

verdicts.quote_a: Expected event cost = events × 17% litigated × $135k mean paid claim
verdicts.quote_b: the mean paid claim is about $133k–136k
verdicts.explanation: The abstract's $135k point value lies inside the protocol's $133k-136k range, and both cite the same two closed-claim analyses (2013 and 2023). That is rounding, not a revision.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the protocol's range of about $133k-136k with its two citations, and note that the abstract's model uses $135k from within it.

verdicts.quote_a: an OR minute costs $34–37 before physician fees (2014 dollars, 30–40% more today)
verdicts.quote_b: at an operating-room cost of $33.78 median / $37.45 mean per minute, FY2014, before physician fees
verdicts.explanation: The abstract's $34-37 rounds the protocol's $33.78 median and $37.45 mean, both in 2014 dollars before physician fees. The base value agrees. The difference is that the abstract's model then multiplies by 1.35 to reach 2026 dollars, with no source for that factor.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry $33.78 median / $37.45 mean per OR minute (FY2014, before physician fees) from the protocol or grant. Mark the abstract's 1.35 inflation factor as unsourced.

verdicts.quote_a: a pre-placed fiducial that itself costs $1,750–1,950 and a second visit
verdicts.quote_b: that is $1,750–1,950 per placement
verdicts.explanation: The grant gets $1,750-1,950 by multiplying the 51.9-minute mean placement time by the 2014 OR-minute cost, so the figure is the OR time of the placement visit itself. The visual abstract says the fiducial 'itself costs' that amount 'and a second visit', which presents the time cost as the fiducial's own cost on top of the visit. Read that way, it counts the visit twice.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the grant's derivation: about $1,750-1,950 per placement, which is 51.9 minutes of OR time at the FY2014 cost, not a price for the device.

verdicts.quote_a: one centre placed 179 preoperative gold fiducials over 38 months, 176 thoracic, at a mean of 51.9 min and 183 mGy each
verdicts.quote_b: at a mean of 52 minutes and 183 mGy each
verdicts.explanation: Both describe the same 2023 single-centre series of 179 placements (176 thoracic) over 38 months. The 18 September 2026 note rounds 51.9 minutes to 52. Same study, same values.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry 51.9 minutes and 183 mGy from the grant, which cites the series in full.

verdicts.quote_a: operating-room minutes (about ten a case, $140k–$500k a year at 300–1,000 cases)
verdicts.quote_b: the 15 comes from two small non-randomised thoracic series and is applied to all cases: the weakest input here
verdicts.explanation: Both use ten minutes a case and $140k-$500k a year at 300-1,000 cases: the abstract's model is N × 10 minutes, priced at $140k-$150k to $460k-$500k. The values agree. The only difference is that the abstract says the input rests on two small thoracic series and calls it the weakest input, while the proposal gives the figure without that caveat.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry ten minutes a case with the abstract's caveat: it comes from two small non-randomised thoracic series (19 and 26 patients) and is applied to every case.

verdicts.quote_a: Review type: Exempt , Category 4, with limited IRB review for privacy and confidentiality because identifiable health information is accessed
verdicts.quote_b: the data from this study may be included in a future 510(k) pre-submission (checklist, FDA row), so the Exempt route is closed
verdicts.explanation: The 15 September 2026 draft of Protocol 1 asks for Exempt Category 4 with limited review. The retrospective protocol is the later Protocol 1: it treats the AIDaS application (deadline 16 October 2026) as planned and refers to the grant's Q2/Q3 timeline. It asks for Expedited Category 5 and gives reasons, keeping the Exempt paragraphs only in case the IRB disagrees. It also says the WSU form applies limited review only to Exempt Categories 2 and 3.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry Expedited Category 5 from the Retrospective Fluoroscopy Protocol. Note that its FDA-ineligibility reason cites no regulation (see candidate 48).

verdicts.quote_a: (Exempt Category 4 or Expedited Category 5; waiver of consent and of HIPAA authorization
verdicts.quote_b: If the IRB nonetheless determines that Exempt Category 4 applies, the Exempt paragraphs in the form are completed for that purpose.
verdicts.explanation: The candidate's quote from the grant is not in it as worded, but the grant does say 'Exempt Category 4 or Expedited Category 5'. The protocol requests Expedited Category 5 and keeps Exempt Category 4 as the IRB's alternative, completing those paragraphs too. The grant's open pair contains the protocol's request and its fallback, so the two are compatible rather than in conflict.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry Expedited Category 5 as requested, with Exempt Category 4 as the IRB's possible alternative, as the Retrospective Fluoroscopy Protocol states.

verdicts.quote_a: Records and images run from 1 January 2006 to the IRB approval date; nothing is collected prospectively.
verdicts.quote_b: spine operations performed between 2021 and 2026, remove all patient identifiers, and use them to train and test the counting method
verdicts.explanation: The 15 September 2026 draft asks for 40,000 imaging studies from about 25,000 patients, 2006 to approval, covering CT, radiographs, MRI, fluoroscopy and the trauma registry. The later retrospective protocol narrows this to one DMC neurosurgeon's spine operations from 2021 to 2026 with archived fluoroscopy, and leaves the case count to a pilot PACS query. It is a redesign of the same Protocol 1.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the retrospective protocol's scope (one surgeon's spine cases, 2021-2026, N to confirm by pilot query). Treat the 2006 window and the 40,000-study figure as the superseded design.

verdicts.quote_a: over the three -year study period
verdicts.quote_b: suggest two years after approval to cover analysis and publication
verdicts.explanation: The September draft runs its analysis steps over a three-year study period. The later retrospective protocol puts extraction, de-identification and annotation in the first three months, fine-tuning and evaluation in months 4-6 and the remainder of the study for write-up, and proposes an end date two years after approval (still to confirm). The grant's project period is one calendar year, 2027.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the retrospective protocol's plan (steps 2-11 within six months, proposed end two years after approval, to confirm). Leave out the draft's three years.

verdicts.quote_a: agree with the level recorded in the operative note and with the CT-verified numbering in at least 98% of vertebrae
verdicts.quote_b: The surgeon's operative note tells us which level was actually operated on, so we can check whether the method counts correctly.
verdicts.explanation: The September draft builds its reference standard by registering each intraoperative frame to the patient's CT, and hypothesises that these labels agree in at least 98% of vertebrae. The later retrospective protocol takes level truth from the operative note, with post-operative imaging where the note is ambiguous; it collects no registered frames, and its primary endpoint is detector recall of at least 97%. The design has changed, and the lift-before-label note's plan for registered frames from Protocol 1 now has no source.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the retrospective protocol's reference standard (operative note, post-operative imaging where needed) and its H1 of at least 97% recall. Mark the CT-registration standard as the earlier design.

verdicts.quote_a: To bound a per-vertebra accuracy of 99% with a 95% interval of ±0.5 percentage points requires about 1,500 verified vertebrae in each primary stratum
verdicts.quote_b: so about 1,100 labelled bodies are needed in the held-out set. (To hold 99% recall to a half-width of 0.5 points would need about 1,520.)
verdicts.explanation: The September draft sizes the study at about 1,500 verified vertebrae in each of four strata, 6,000 in all, at 99% ±0.5. The later protocol sizes one held-out set at about 1,100 bodies for 97% recall ±1 point, and cites the old 99% rule only for comparison. The strata and the higher bar are gone.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry about 1,100 labelled held-out bodies (97%, half-width 1 point) from the Retrospective Fluoroscopy Protocol. Note that its case count waits on the 20-case pilot query.

verdicts.quote_a: Fine-tuned on a few thousand annotated in-domain frames, the fluoroscopy detector should reach the film detector's range on held-out cases from the same devices
verdicts.quote_b: A detector fine-tuned on DMC fluoroscopy will reach per-body recall of at least 97% on held-out DMC cases (target 95% CI half-width 1 point)
verdicts.explanation: The proposal expects the film detector's range, about 99.14%. The protocol's hypothesis is a floor of at least 97%, and the same sentence cites the 99.14% as context. An expectation near 99% and a hypothesis of 'at least 97%' are compatible. They are a prediction and a test threshold, not two conflicting values.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the protocol's H1 (at least 97%) as the pre-specified bar, and the proposal's 99.14% as the expectation it is compared against.

verdicts.quote_a: roughly 1,500–2,500 intraoperative images from 800–1,500 patients
verdicts.quote_b: Target 3,000-5,000 frames from 800-1,500 patients in twelve months at one centre
verdicts.explanation: Both pages are dated 15 September 2026 and plan the same retrospective PACS pull from the same 800-1,500 patients. The protocol draft expects 1,500-2,500 images; the FluoroCap note targets 3,000-5,000 frames and plans for about half the cases to be missing from PACS. Neither refers to the other, and the later retrospective protocol leaves frames per case to a 20-case pilot query.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry neither as settled. The pilot PACS query of 20 cases named in the Retrospective Fluoroscopy Protocol (frames per case, share missing from PACS) decides the yield.

verdicts.quote_a: Protocol 2 (prospective silent evaluation) is unchanged and is submitted alongside.
verdicts.quote_b: it is not part of this submission and will be submitted as a separate protocol if this study meets its endpoints
verdicts.explanation: The 15 September 2026 draft submits Protocol 2 alongside Protocol 1. The later retrospective protocol says the shadow-mode study is not part of the submission and will follow as a separate protocol only if Protocol 1 meets its endpoints. That matches the grant, which runs the shadow-mode study in Q3 2027 under a second protocol.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the retrospective protocol's sequence: Protocol 2 is submitted separately, after Protocol 1 meets its endpoints.

verdicts.quote_a: Unfunded / departmental. If NIH or other support is added later, update.
verdicts.quote_b: Award requested: $20,000 for a one-year project period, January 1 to December 31, 2027.
verdicts.explanation: The grant is a request, not an award. The later retrospective protocol still answers 'Does this project have funding? N' and calls the AIDaS application planned, with notification on 16 December 2026, to be added by amendment if awarded. 'Unfunded' and 'requested' agree.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry 'no funding at submission; AIDaS seed grant applied for, to be amended in if awarded', as the Retrospective Fluoroscopy Protocol words it.

verdicts.quote_a: eProtocol requires a faculty sponsor/mentor for a resident PI
verdicts.quote_b: is a resident and is not eligible to serve as PI.
verdicts.explanation: The candidate's quote is not in the draft as worded; the draft lists the resident as PGY-1 Surgery at DMC and notes that a resident PI needs a faculty sponsor. The grant's ineligibility comes from the AIDaS call, which requires tenure-track or tenured faculty. These rules belong to two different instruments, the IRB form and the seed grant, so they do not contradict each other. The later retrospective protocol leaves the IRB PI open on exactly that question.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the two rules separately: the AIDaS call needs a faculty PI, and the IRB PI is still to be decided (Retrospective Fluoroscopy Protocol). Separately, check the draft's 'PGY-1 Surgery' against the grant's 'neurosurgery resident'.

verdicts.quote_a: The existing Not Human Participant Research determination 2026_269 covers public de-identified data only, so this is a new protocol.
verdicts.quote_b: outside WSU determination 2026-269, covered by its supplement HPR 2026-330 (notice 2026-09-29)
verdicts.explanation: The atlas (17 October 2026) records VinDr, a named-person data-use dataset, as outside 2026-269 and covered by a separate supplement, HPR 2026-330. That does not widen 2026-269 itself, and nothing extends either determination to DMC PACS data, so the grant's conclusion that PACS data need a new protocol still holds. The pages also spell the id two ways (2026_269 and 2026-269).
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the grant's statement, adding that supplement HPR 2026-330 (notice 2026-09-29) covers VinDr. Use one spelling of the determination id.

verdicts.quote_a: Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.22642578
verdicts.quote_b: Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.22139642
verdicts.explanation: The 15 September 2026 draft and the 8 October 2026 handoff give different Zenodo DOIs for the same CTSpinoPelvic1K release. Zenodo issues both a concept DOI and per-version DOIs, so both could be valid, and neither page says which kind it gives.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Settle it by resolving both DOIs on Zenodo to see whether one is the concept record and the other a version (and which version, v10 or v11). Then cite the concept DOI, or the version the work used.

verdicts.quote_a: a public CT dataset of 802 abdominopelvic scans
verdicts.quote_b: 6,234/6,255 (99.66%) on 801 abdominopelvic spines
verdicts.explanation: The draft counts the scans released; the grant counts the spines in one counting arm. Counting From The Sacrum (22 September 2026) says the CT axis 'named 802 abdominopelvic records' and now counts CTSpinoPelvic1K by distinct subject as 801. The atlas records 801 renders, or 802 in banks rebuilt after a 23 September repair. The two numbers count different things.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry 802 records for the release and 801 for the counting arm (distinct subjects), stating the difference.

verdicts.quote_a: On real intraoperative C-arm lateral frames the method names the exact level in 98.2% of vertebrae.
verdicts.quote_b: 97.4 % of bodies named on a whole lateral frame and 74.8 % with one body in view
verdicts.explanation: On 22 September 2026 the page gives 98.22% exact on whole lateral frames and 72.85% with one vertebra. On 8 October 2026 the handoff gives 97.4% and 74.8%. Research Directions (also 8 October) puts the count alone at 97.0% and coupling at 98.2% in the same setting, so 98.2% and 97.4% may be different quantities rather than old and new values of one. The person-level held-out rule of 23 September may also have changed the denominator.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Settle it with paper 1's claims file, which defines 97.4% and 98.2% and gives each one's held-out rule and denominator. Then carry the 8 October figure if it is the same measure, re-scored.

verdicts.quote_a: | Lateral, whole frame 141 cases, 617 vertebrae, 5-fold CV |
verdicts.quote_b: 98.2% exact level on whole C-ArmLSpine lateral frames, five-fold CV over 148 cases [95.7–100]
verdicts.explanation: Both pages are dated 22 September 2026 and give the same whole-frame lateral result (98.2%, lower bound 95.7%) from the same five-fold cross-validation. One says 141 cases, the other 148. The ledger's split table (105/15/28) sums to 148, while Counting From The Sacrum counts C-ArmLSpine as 120 distinct subjects, and the atlas lists 149 sessions 'not provably one person each'.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Settle it with the fold lists of the cross-validation (cases with a lateral frame scored). Until then, carry 98.2% with the case count marked unresolved (141 or 148 cases; 120 distinct subjects).

verdicts.quote_a: Under the matched convention the C-ArmLSpine-held-out vertebra recall is 90.6%.
verdicts.quote_b: held-out-device detection recall 80.5 %; same-device plateau about 84 %
verdicts.explanation: The ledger (22 September 2026) re-scores the C-ArmLSpine-held-out detector at 90.6% on 56 whole frames under outline boxes, with the same-device pooled arm at 90.6% under body boxes. The handoff (8 October 2026) gives 80.5% for held-out-device recall and a same-device plateau of about 84%, which it calls 'the truth denominator: 95.6 % on repaired boxes'. The handoff names neither the device, the box convention nor the frames.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Settle it with paper 1's claims file: which device was held out for 80.5%, under which box convention and denominator. Until then, carry the ledger's 90.6% with its convention stated.

verdicts.quote_a: On public labelled CT renders and real radiographs with annotation boxes, the count was exact on 99.17–100% of reached walks
verdicts.quote_b: C2 on a real image is not demonstrated.
verdicts.explanation: The grant's 1,205 of 1,209 walks from C2 on 262 real radiographs are scored with the annotation's boxes, as the paragraph says. The ledger's statement is about the learned detector finding C2 (0-8% of 25 labelled instances). One is counting given true boxes, the other is detection, so the scopes differ. The grant itself says the deployment risk is detection.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry both with their scopes: counting from C2 is exact on 99.67% of walks given annotation boxes, and a learned C2 detector on real film is not demonstrated (OR Readiness Ledger).

verdicts.quote_a: A detector trained on real films reaches 99.14% per-body recall on real radiographs
verdicts.quote_b: but 17.9% come out duplicated , and that duplication traces to a rule in our own linking code, not to the detector
verdicts.explanation: The 18 September 2026 note blames the 17.9% duplication on a linking rule, not on the detector, so it does not lower detector recall. But the same note gives two detection figures, 'misses only 2.2%' on real film and 99.2% with 'three misses in 243' (about 98.8%), and neither matches 99.14% exactly. The pages do not say which test sets these figures come from.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Settle it with the evaluation records naming the test set behind 99.14%, 99.2% (3 of 243) and the 2.2% miss rate. Report the duplication as a linking defect, not a detector one.

verdicts.quote_a: The innovation is to count, not name.
verdicts.quote_b: This method never counts — it matches the spot film onto a map built minutes earlier from the patient's own spine
verdicts.explanation: The 18 September 2026 internal summary describes naming a spot film by matching it onto a sweep map, and says outright that the method never counts. Counting Levels Under Fluoroscopy (runs of 21 September), the October 2026 grant and the retrospective protocol all describe counting from an anchor, with no name formed. The later documents describe the method now proposed.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry 'count, not name' from the grant and the protocol as the method under validation. Treat Vertebral Levels Without CT as an earlier, naming-based design.

verdicts.quote_a: No public dataset of intraoperative spine fluoroscopy with vertebra-level labels exists.
verdicts.quote_b: No labels and no poses ship with the release.
verdicts.explanation: The atlas (17 October 2026) records that C-ArmLSpine ships no labels. Its 814-of-910 agreed levels are project-derived, from TotalSegmentator and SPINEPS on each CBCT, and the record says level_labels false. SX-Stitch is listed as a private request with vertebra masks. The atlas therefore supports the draft's statement rather than contradicting it.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Keep the draft's statement, adding from the atlas that C-ArmLSpine supplies CBCT pairs from which this project derived its own level labels.

verdicts.quote_a: placed labels correctly on 398 of 398 intraoperative radiographs from 178 patients; it requires a CT and is not publicly available
verdicts.quote_b: labels fell within the correct level in all cases
verdicts.explanation: The deep-research note of 15 September 2026 gives the same 398 radiographs from 178 patients, all within the correct level, after 21 further films were excluded for invisible vertebral boundaries. Its arithmetic that does not reconcile (157 against 168) belongs to the separate helpfulness survey, not to labelling accuracy. The accuracy figures agree; the draft just leaves out the exclusion.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry 398 of 398 with its caveat from the Registration-Free Level ID Feasibility note: 100% after excluding 21 films, cervical repositioning cases excluded, single institution.

verdicts.quote_a: the best found is 88.3% on 100 cadaver Long-Film images from a network trained only on images synthesised from 297 CTs
verdicts.quote_b: (88.3% labelling, F1 > 96%, 3.3 mm, lateral 35 points worse single-view) did NOT survive verification and are not asserted here
verdicts.explanation: Both pages are dated 15 September 2026. The FluoroCap note uses the 2022 cadaver study's 88.3% as the best CT-free comparator. The adversarially verified feasibility note says that figure did not survive verification (refuted 0-3) and keeps only the description of the study's protocol.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Do not carry 88.3% as a verified comparator. Describe the 2022 study by its protocol alone, as the Registration-Free Level ID Feasibility note does.

verdicts.quote_a: That contradicts the directive that FluoroCap is out of every training set
verdicts.quote_b: dropped by directive; the 200-panel test set does not exist
verdicts.explanation: The 8 October 2026 handoff does not say FluoroCap is out of every training set. It says the directive requires that, and records as a defect that the C-ArmLSpine fold banks still hold 2,100 FluoroCap crops each. The same-day Research Directions note records the directive and the missing test set, and proposes a design with FluoroCap in no training list. Neither page claims the defect has been fixed, so they do not conflict.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the handoff's record: FluoroCap is out by directive, but the C-ArmLSpine fold banks behind the fine-tuned naming numbers still hold FluoroCap and VinDr crops, until a retrain is recorded.

verdicts.quote_a: Every saved fluoroscopic series from spine cases, 2021–2026
verdicts.quote_b: at one university centre 90 of 190 consecutive cases had intraoperative images only on film or outside PACS
verdicts.explanation: The proposal plans to collect every saved series; it does not claim every case has one. The draft's 90 of 190 is a caution from a different centre, given in its notes as a reason to ask Radiology whether C-arm saves reach PACS. The two statements are about different things and do not conflict.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the plan as stated, with the draft's caution that at another centre about half of cases had no PACS images. The pilot PACS query settles DMC's share.

verdicts.quote_a: every prerequisite has a fixed lead time of fifteen business days, so the paperwork is the critical path.
verdicts.quote_b: dosimetry badges, Appendix L training form and Dosimetry Request Form filed ≥15 business days ahead
verdicts.explanation: The proposal states the fifteen-business-day lead time with no source. The grant attributes it to 'the OEHS Radiation Safety policy' by name only, with no document, section or link, and the retrospective protocol repeats it the same way. None of the three pages cites a source a reader could check.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Cite the OEHS Radiation Safety policy document and its section on dosimetry and training lead times before the textbook carries the fifteen days.

verdicts.quote_a: The Joint Commission recorded 127 wrong surgeries in 2024, nine wrong-level and seven spinal, with severe permanent harm in 36%.
verdicts.quote_b: NHS England recorded 185 wrong-site never events in 2024/25
verdicts.explanation: In both the grant and the retrospective protocol, the Joint Commission figures (127, 9, 7, 36%) and the NHS England figure (185) carry only the organisation's name, with no report title or date. Every neighbouring figure in the same paragraphs carries a full citation. The visual abstract lists 'Joint Commission Sentinel Event Data 2024' without the 36% figure.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Cite the Joint Commission's 2024 sentinel event report and NHS England's 2024/25 never-events data, and check the 36% harm figure in them.

verdicts.quote_a: Navigation = $1.5M capital over 7 years plus 10% service, an assumption, not a source
verdicts.quote_b: Also not known: a verified capital cost for a navigation suite, any study showing that navigation reduces wrong-level surgery
verdicts.explanation: The abstract labels its navigation cost an assumption ('vendor pricing') and says no published study shows navigation reduces wrong-level surgery. The grant and the protocol state the same absences. None of the pages describes a search that would back the claim that no such evidence exists.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Record the search behind the absence claims (databases, terms, date) before the textbook carries them; otherwise carry them as 'not found by the authors'.

verdicts.quote_a: synthetic fluoroscopy from CT is close in physics but tuned to one C-arm and one cadaveric population.
verdicts.quote_b: Synthetic fluoroscopy is therefore close in physics but tuned to one C-arm and one population.
verdicts.explanation: Both pages give the sentence as the conclusion of evidence they set out just before it: 366 DeepFluoro frames of six cadaveric pelves on one Siemens Cios Fusion, the variance figures, and the gap between population-matched and other-CT detectors. The basis is stated on the page, so the claim is not unsourced.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the conclusion with its stated basis (DeepFluoro, one Cios Fusion, six cadavers). The OR Readiness Ledger's results on other devices can be cited as further support.

verdicts.quote_a: DMC archives intraoperative fluoroscopy to PACS for at least one neurosurgical service, and most spine-surgery patients have a pre- or post-operative CT
verdicts.quote_b: spine cases 2021–2026, with level truth from operative notes and post-operative imaging
verdicts.explanation: The claim that most spine-surgery patients have a CT appears only in the 15 September 2026 draft. The grant claims nothing about CT; it takes level truth from operative notes and post-operative imaging. All the two pages share is that DMC fluoroscopy is saved to PACS, which is not the claim the candidate names.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Treat CT availability as the draft's own unverified premise. The retrospective protocol's pilot PACS query (cases, frames, post-operative imaging) is what would measure coverage.

verdicts.quote_a: cadaver work is not human-subjects research and needs no IRB, only the program's and biosafety approval.
verdicts.quote_b: not human-subjects research under the Common Rule
verdicts.explanation: Both pages say cadaver work through the Body Bequest Program needs only a program proposal and biosafety approval, not an IRB. The grant names the Common Rule but cites no WSU policy, and its $1,000-3,000 cadaver fee is marked to confirm. Neither page gives a source for the approval route or the fee.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Cite the Body Bequest Program's research policy (or the WSU IRB's guidance on decedent research) and get the program's current fee before the textbook carries either.

verdicts.quote_a: research that may support an FDA submission is not eligible for exemption
verdicts.quote_b: The WSU form applies limited IRB review to Exempt Categories 2 and 3 only
verdicts.explanation: The retrospective protocol cites 45 CFR 46.104(d)(4) and 46.110 for the two review types. But it gives no regulation or WSU policy for its decisive claim that research that may support an FDA submission cannot be exempt; it points only to its own checklist's FDA row. Its statement about which exempt categories the WSU form gives limited review is also unsourced.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Cite the WSU IRB policy or the 21 CFR 56 provision behind the FDA-ineligibility rule, and the eProtocol help text for the limited-review categories.

verdicts.quote_a: the fraction of cases on which a full count is possible is unknown and is expected to be a minority [to confirm]
verdicts.explanation: The claim is only in the retrospective protocol. The proposal's quoted line is about what the method can guarantee, a measured bound at a stated decline rate. It says nothing about how many archived cases allow a count. The claim is not shared.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the protocol's statement as its own pre-stated limitation; only the pilot query and the decline rate will measure it.

verdicts.quote_a: The median NPDB payment for a surgical never event is $75,220 (IQR $28,847–$215,003, 2025 dollars
verdicts.quote_b: The National Practitioner Data Bank median payment for a surgical never event is $75,220 (IQR $28,847–$215,003, 2025 dollars)
verdicts.explanation: The grant's significance paragraph and the protocol's background paragraph carry the same sequence of figures, nearly word for word: registry 0.12% and 81.3%, 1 in 3,110, 50% of 415, 17% of 418, nearly 20% of 569, 81% of 68 litigated, $75,220 median, £535.5M and the Joint Commission counts. It is one claim carried twice, not two confirmations.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Keep one master copy (the protocol's carries fuller citations). Correct the registry description and the 81.3% reading in both places at once.

verdicts.quote_a: The only learned component finds vertebral bodies and the anchor in a frame; nothing learned decides the level.
verdicts.quote_b: The only learned component is a detector of vertebral bodies and the anchor class. Nothing learned decides the level
verdicts.explanation: The proposal, the grant and the protocol carry the same method sentence and the same 0.6-body correlation window. The grant still lists whether that window holds against manual step error as an open question for the phantom sweeps. This is one description repeated, not independent support.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the method description once, with the grant's note that the 0.6-body window is untested against manual step error.

verdicts.quote_a: from the sacrum, second-institution spines | | 522 | | 7,168 / 7,228 | | 99.17%
verdicts.quote_b: 7,168/7,228 (99.17%) on 522 second-institution spines
verdicts.explanation: The proposal's table and the grant's paragraph carry the same five arms (834/834, 1,205/1,209, 6,234/6,255, 7,168/7,228, 99.31% of 5,385). The grant adds confidence intervals and the 98.57% of 6,343. Both cite the same manuscript in preparation, so they are one result, not two.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the grant's version, which has intervals and the sixth confirmation arm, cited to the manuscript in preparation.

verdicts.quote_a: three seeds of one dataset spanned 26 points
verdicts.quote_b: trained on renders of other living whole-body CTs it finds it on about 64–77%, and three training seeds of one dataset spanned 26 points
verdicts.explanation: The grant and the protocol carry the same DeepFluoro paragraph: 366 frames, six pelves, 80.9%, 93.9%, a 99.5% ceiling, about 96-98%, about 64-77% and the 26-point seed spread. It includes the 80.9% and 96-98% that candidates 0 and 2 dispute, so one correction has to be made in both places.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Correct both copies together, using the 86%/about 90% physics reading and the 90-97% sacrum range from Counting Levels Under Fluoroscopy.

verdicts.quote_a: Wrong-level spine surgery is 1 in 830 operations in a 34,544-case registry (1 in 240 in the thoracic spine), and half of surveyed spine surgeons have done it once; 81% of events are a count that went wrong under fluoroscopy
verdicts.quote_b: 81% of events are intraoperative disorientation — a count that went wrong
verdicts.explanation: The proposal's TL;DR and the abstract's headline carry the same four figures (1 in 830, 1 in 240 thoracic, half of surveyed surgeons, 81%). The abstract cites the registry paper, the 2008 survey and the 2013 survey; the proposal gives no citation inline. It is one claim carried twice.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the figures once with the abstract's citations, and use the grant's wording 'intraoperative disorientation' for the 81% (see candidate 8).

verdicts.quote_a: It addresses screw placement; no published study shows it reduces wrong-level surgery.
verdicts.quote_b: Not available in the literature, and stated so here: a verified capital cost of a navigation suite, any study showing that navigation reduces wrong-level surgery
verdicts.explanation: The candidate's quote from the protocol is about in-domain fluoroscopy, not navigation. The protocol's background does carry the same navigation absences as the abstract and the grant: no verified capital cost and no study showing navigation reduces wrong-level surgery. It is one unsourced comparison repeated, and in the IRB document it is pitch material.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Carry the navigation comparison once, from the grant or abstract, with the search that backs it (see candidate 44). The IRB protocol does not need it.

verdicts.quote_a: Every synthetic-data number here is from the leave-one-specimen-out runs of 21 September 2026
verdicts.quote_b: every number so far is from synthetic CPU runs
verdicts.explanation: The grid pipeline page (21 October 2026) counts zero jobs for the new SchwingNet gate pipeline, which waits on one press in Beethoven. The OR readiness ledger shows many earlier grid jobs, so that zero does not mean nothing ran on the grid before. No page records whether the phantom sweeps or the cadaver session that the September proposal said to start 'this week' have begun.
verdicts.resolution_hint: Settle it with a record of the OEHS/DLAR paperwork and of any phantom or cadaver session. Until then, carry the proposal's numbers as dated 21 September 2026.

verdicts.quote_a: Submission: single PDF, submitted per the RFP [to confirm: address] , by October 16, 2026, 11:59 p.m. ET.
verdicts.quote_b: deadline October 16, 2026; notification December 16, 2026) is planned
verdicts.explanation: The grant's deadline was 16 October 2026, and the draft still holds placeholders for the PI, the address and budget lines 1-5. The protocol only calls the application planned. No page records whether the proposal was submitted, or with which faculty PI.

verdicts.quote_a: [to confirm: mean number of archived intraoperative frames per case, from a pilot query of 20 cases]
verdicts.quote_b: A second team member checks every frame of a random [to confirm: verification fraction of cases; 10% proposed] of cases
